summary: Check exact statements of the concentration/bootstrap theorems the paper cites

checks.exact_statement:
All page/numbering references below were verified against a full text of the OUP 2013 edition (483-PDF-page scan; PDF page = printed page + 9), cross-checked against the printed table of contents.

(1) CONFIRMED — Corollary 2.6, printed p. 33, at the end of Section 2.5 "A maximal inequality" (Section 2.5 runs pp. 30–33; the running head on p. 33 reads "Hoeffding's inequality" because Section 2.6 starts on the same page).

Exact statement (verbatim, verified against the rendered page image):
"Corollary 2.6  Let Z_1, ..., Z_N be real-valued random variables belonging to Γ_+(v,c) (see Section 2.4 for the definition). Then
    E max_{i=1,...,N} Z_i ≤ sqrt(2v log N) + c log N ."

Three details that matter for a paper:
 - The hypothesis is membership in Γ_+(v,c) (sub-gamma on the RIGHT tail), which in BLM's Section 2.4 definition presupposes the variables are CENTERED (E Z_i = 0).
 - NO independence is assumed. Corollary 2.6 follows from Theorem 2.5 (p. 32), which needs only ψ_{Z_i}(λ) ≤ ψ(λ) for each i, plus a union bound inside the expectation.
 - "log" is the natural logarithm throughout BLM.

Supporting context, Theorem 2.5 (p. 32): if ψ_{Z_i}(λ) ≤ ψ(λ) for all λ ∈ (0,b) and all i, with ψ convex, continuously differentiable on [0,b), ψ(0) = ψ'(0) = 0, then E max_{i≤N} Z_i ≤ ψ*^{-1}(log N); in particular for sub-Gaussian Z_i with variance factor v (ψ(λ) = λ²v/2), E max_{i≤N} Z_i ≤ sqrt(2v log N). Corollary 2.6 is the specialization ψ(λ) = vλ²/(2(1-cλ)), using ψ*^{-1}(u) = sqrt(2vu) + cu computed on p. 29.

(2) CONFIRMED, with a precision. BLM DEFINE sub-gamma via the mgf; the tail form is a derived consequence, and the "characterization" is only approximate.

Definition, Section 2.4, printed p. 27 (verbatim): a real-valued CENTERED random variable X is said to be sub-gamma on the right tail with variance factor v and scale parameter c if
    ψ_X(λ) ≤ λ²v / (2(1 - cλ))   for every λ such that 0 < λ < 1/c,
where ψ_X(λ) = log E e^{λX}. The collection is denoted Γ_+(v,c). Γ_-(v,c) is defined by applying this to -X; Γ(v,c) = Γ_+(v,c) ∩ Γ_-(v,c); and BLM note Γ(v,0) = G(v) (the sub-Gaussian class).

Derived tail form, p. 29: BLM compute ψ*(t) = (v/c²) h_1(ct/v) with h_1(u) = 1 + u - sqrt(1+2u) (their eq. (2.5)), invert it to ψ*^{-1}(u) = sqrt(2vu) + cu, and conclude via Chernoff that for X sub-gamma on the right tail, for every t > 0
    P{X > t} ≤ exp(-(v/c²) h_1(ct/v)),   "or equivalently, for every t > 0,   P{X > sqrt(2vt) + ct} ≤ e^{-t}."
For X ∈ Γ(v,c) the same bound holds for -X.

Approximate converse, Theorem 2.3 (p. 29): the two-sided tail condition P{X > sqrt(2vt)+ct} ∨ P{-X > sqrt(2vt)+ct} ≤ e^{-t} for all t > 0 implies E[X^{2q}] ≤ q!(8v)^q + (2q)!(4c)^{2q}; conversely E[X^{2q}] ≤ q!A^q + (2q)!B^{2q} implies X ∈ Γ(4(A+B²), 2B). So the tail form "essentially characterizes" sub-gamma variables only up to absolute constants in v and c — it is NOT literally equivalent to the mgf definition.

The Bernstein-type tail P{X > t} ≤ exp(-t²/(2(v+ct))) IS in the book and IS implied by the sub-gamma mgf condition, but it is strictly weaker. It appears as Corollary 2.11, printed p. 37 (stated for S = sum of centered independent X_i under the moment conditions of Theorem 2.10):
    P{S ≥ t} ≤ exp(-t² / (2(v + ct))).
Its proof is exactly the sub-gamma computation: h_1(u) ≥ u²/(2(1+u)) for u > 0 (Exercise 2.8), hence ψ*_S(t) ≥ t²/(2(v+ct)), then Chernoff. The same three lines apply verbatim to any X ∈ Γ_+(v,c). Direction of implication (I verified the algebra): substituting t = sqrt(2vs) + cs into t²/(2(v+ct)) gives s·(2v + 2c·sqrt(2vs) + c²s)/(2v + 2c·sqrt(2vs) + 2c²s) ≤ s, so the exp(-t²/(2(v+ct))) form is implied by, but does not recover, P{X > sqrt(2vs)+cs} ≤ e^{-s}. It does recover it with c doubled: P{X > sqrt(2vs) + 2cs} ≤ e^{-s}. So: "implied, and equivalent only up to a factor 2 in the scale parameter."

(3) REFUTED as stated. BLM does state a finite-N lower bound for the maximum of independent standard Gaussians, but the constant is 1/sqrt(2), not 1/sqrt(π log 2), and it is Exercise 13.6 (Chapter 13), not anything in Chapter 2.

Exercise 13.6, printed p. 385 (Section 13.11 "Exercises" of Chapter 13, "The expected value of suprema of empirical processes"), verified from the rendered page image:
"Exercise 13.6 (EXPECTATION OF A MAXIMUM OF INDEPENDENT GAUSSIAN RANDOM VARIABLES.) Let (X_s)_{s∈T} be independent standard Gaussian random variables. Prove that for |T| ≥ 2,
    E max_{s∈T} X_s ≥ (1/sqrt(2)) sqrt(log |T|) ."

This is used in the proof of Theorem 13.4 (Sudakov's lower bound), printed p. 356, where BLM write "E sup_{t∈T} Z_t ≥ (1/sqrt(2)) sqrt(log |T|)" for independent standard Gaussians and say the proof "is left as exercise (Exercise 13.6)". Theorem 13.4 itself reads: for a finite T and a centered Gaussian vector (X_t)_{t∈T},
    E sup_{t∈T} X_t ≥ (1/2) · min_{t≠t'∈T} sqrt(E[(X_t - X_{t'})²]) · sqrt(log |T|).

The only other Chapter-2 statement about the sharpness of the Gaussian maximum is Exercise 2.17, printed p. 48, which is ASYMPTOTIC, not a finite-N lower bound:
"Exercise 2.17  Let G_1, ..., G_N be independent standard normal random variables. Then lim_{N→∞} E max_{i=1,...,N} G_i / sqrt(2 log N) = 1. (See Galambos (1987).)"
The main text on p. 30 refers to this as showing the sqrt(2v log N) bound "is asymptotically sharp if the Z_i are i.i.d. normal random variables, see Exercise 2.17."

I grepped the entire book text for every lower bound of the form "E max/sup ... ≥ ... log": there are exactly three hits (Theorem 13.4, its proof, and Exercise 13.6). The constant 1/sqrt(π log 2) does not appear anywhere in the book.
checks.corrections:
Item (1): correct as you stated it, with three refinements to add. (a) Cite it as Corollary 2.6, p. 33, and locate it in Section 2.5 ("A maximal inequality", pp. 30–33) — do not call it a Section 2.6 result; Section 2.6 is Hoeffding's inequality. (b) Do not say "each X_i is sub-gamma"; BLM's notation is Z_i ∈ Γ_+(v,c), i.e. sub-gamma ON THE RIGHT TAIL, and BLM's definition builds in E Z_i = 0. If your variables are not centered, the corollary bounds E max_i (Z_i - E Z_i), not E max_i Z_i. (c) Do NOT assume independence is required — it is not, which is usually the reason one cites this result rather than an extreme-value argument. Saying "for independent sub-gamma variables" understates the result and is a common miscitation.

Item (2): your framing is slightly off. BLM DEFINE the class by the mgf bound log E e^{λX} ≤ λ²v/(2(1-cλ)) for 0 < λ < 1/c (Section 2.4, p. 27), and DERIVE P{X > sqrt(2vt) + ct} ≤ e^{-t} (p. 29) via the Cramér–Chernoff method. So "the book uses the mgf form as the definition and the sqrt(2vt)+ct tail as a corollary" is the accurate statement. The tail form is not equivalent to the mgf form: the converse (Theorem 2.3, p. 29) loses constants — the two-sided tail condition with (v,c) only yields membership in Γ(4(A+B²), 2B) after passing through even moments. Say "essentially characterizes, up to absolute constants" rather than "equivalent". The form P(X > t) ≤ exp(-t²/(2(v+ct))) is in the book as Corollary 2.11 (p. 37, Bernstein), it IS implied by the sub-gamma mgf condition (via h_1(u) ≥ u²/(2(1+u)), Exercise 2.8), but it is strictly weaker than the sqrt(2vt)+ct form; it recovers that form only with c replaced by 2c.

Item (3): the substantive error. (a) The constant is WRONG for BLM. BLM's Exercise 13.6 (p. 385) has 1/sqrt(2) ≈ 0.7071, not 1/sqrt(π log 2) ≈ 0.6777. (b) The LOCATION is wrong: it is Exercise 13.6 in Chapter 13, not anywhere in Chapter 2; the Chapter 2 companion (Exercise 2.17, p. 48) is a purely asymptotic limit statement, not a finite-N lower bound. (c) The "sigma" is your addition: BLM state it for standard Gaussians (sigma = 1); the sigma version follows by homogeneity but is not what is printed. (d) A caution if you cite BLM's version at small N: I checked numerically and BLM's Exercise 13.6 as printed is FALSE at |T| = 2 — E max of two i.i.d. N(0,1) is 1/sqrt(π) = 0.564190, whereas sqrt(log 2 / 2) = 0.588705. It holds for |T| ≥ 3 (N=3: 0.84629 vs 0.74115; N=10: 1.53875 vs 1.07298; and asymptotically the truth is sqrt(2 log N)). So the stated "for |T| ≥ 2" range is off by one; it should be |T| ≥ 3. (e) The constant 1/sqrt(π log 2) that you actually want is from Gautam Kamath's widely circulated note "Bounds on the Expectation of the Maximum of Samples from a Gaussian", Theorem 1: for Y = max_{1≤i≤n} X_i with X_i ~ N(0, σ²) i.i.d., (1/sqrt(π log 2))·σ·sqrt(log n) ≤ E[Y] ≤ sqrt(2)·σ·sqrt(log n). That constant is chosen precisely to be tight at n = 2 (it gives exactly σ/sqrt(π) there — I verified: 0.564190 vs 0.564190), which is why it is the right constant to quote if you need validity for all n ≥ 1 or n ≥ 2. Kamath's note is a self-published PDF, not a peer-reviewed source; if you need a citable book result, cite BLM Exercise 13.6 (with |T| ≥ 3) or BLM Theorem 13.4 (Sudakov) instead.
checks.recommended_citation:
For the upper bound (item 1), write something like:

"If Z_1, ..., Z_N are sub-gamma on the right tail with variance factor v and scale parameter c — that is, log E e^{λ Z_i} ≤ λ² v / (2(1 - cλ)) for all 0 < λ < 1/c and all i, in the notation Z_i ∈ Γ_+(v,c) — then E[max_{i ≤ N} Z_i] ≤ sqrt(2 v log N) + c log N. No independence among the Z_i is required. [Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, 2013, Corollary 2.6, p. 33]"

If you also want the sub-Gaussian special case, cite the same place: "[BLM, 2013, Theorem 2.5, p. 32]" gives E[max_{i ≤ N} Z_i] ≤ sqrt(2 v log N) for sub-Gaussian Z_i with variance factor v.

For the sub-gamma definition and tail form (item 2):

"We use the moment-generating-function definition of the sub-gamma class Γ_+(v,c) [BLM, 2013, Section 2.4, p. 27]; the Cramér–Chernoff method yields the equivalent-form tail bound P{Z > sqrt(2vt) + ct} ≤ e^{-t} for all t > 0 [BLM, 2013, p. 29], and the weaker but often more convenient Bernstein form P{Z > t} ≤ exp(-t² / (2(v + ct))) [BLM, 2013, Corollary 2.11, p. 37]."
If you assert a converse, hedge it: "the tail condition characterizes the sub-gamma property up to absolute constants in (v,c) [BLM, 2013, Theorem 2.3, p. 29]."

For the lower bound (item 3), pick one of these three, and do NOT attribute 1/sqrt(π log 2) to BLM:

(i) Book citation, safe range: "For independent standard Gaussian X_1, ..., X_N with N ≥ 3, E[max_{i ≤ N} X_i] ≥ (1/sqrt(2)) sqrt(log N) [BLM, 2013, Exercise 13.6, p. 385]." (Optionally footnote that the exercise is printed for N ≥ 2 but the inequality is tight-to-failing at N = 2, where E[max] = 1/sqrt(π) < sqrt((log 2)/2).)

(ii) All-N constant, non-book source: "For X_1, ..., X_N i.i.d. N(0, σ²), (1/sqrt(π log 2)) σ sqrt(log N) ≤ E[max_{i ≤ N} X_i] ≤ sqrt(2) σ sqrt(log N), the lower constant being tight at N = 2 [Kamath, 'Bounds on the Expectation of the Maximum of Samples from a Gaussian', Theorem 1]."

(iii) Most citable general form: "E[sup_{t ∈ T} X_t] ≥ (1/2) min_{s ≠ t} (E[(X_s - X_t)²])^{1/2} sqrt(log |T|) for a centered Gaussian vector indexed by a finite T [BLM, 2013, Theorem 13.4 (Sudakov's lower bound), p. 356]." For i.i.d. N(0, σ²) the pairwise L² distance is σ sqrt(2), giving E[max_{i ≤ N} X_i] ≥ (σ/sqrt(2)) sqrt(log N) — the same constant as Exercise 13.6.

If you want an asymptotic sharpness remark instead: "E[max_{i ≤ N} G_i] / sqrt(2 log N) → 1 as N → ∞ for i.i.d. standard normals [BLM, 2013, Exercise 2.17, p. 48]."

Bibliographic entry: Stéphane Boucheron, Gábor Lugosi and Pascal Massart, Concentration Inequalities: A Nonasymptotic Theory of Independence, Oxford University Press, 2013 (a corrected paperback edition appeared in 2016; page numbers above are the 2013 edition and match the printed table of contents).

Verified against the arXiv PDF (arXiv:0907.3740v1, the only version, submitted 21 Jul 2009) AND against the authors' own LaTeX e-print source (`svp-final.tex`, retrieved from https://arxiv.org/e-print/0907.3740v1). The COLT 2009 proceedings PDF hosted by Pontil (http://www0.cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/M.Pontil/reading/svp-final.pdf) is compiled from the same source file. Local copies: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Volumes-Crucial-X6-MacBook-Code-ml-papers/86fbc9c4-7358-4aff-9451-5f33ce107df2/scratchpad/mp0907.3740.pdf and .../scratchpad/mpsrc/svp-final.tex

(1) THEOREM NUMBERING — CONFIRMED. Theorem 4 IS the empirical Bernstein bound. In colt09e.sty all environments share one counter (`\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}`, `\newtheorem{corollary}[theorem]{Corollary}`), so the sequence is: Theorem 1 (Hoeffding's inequality), Corollary 2 (Hoeffding, finite class), Theorem 3 (Bennett's inequality), **Theorem 4 (empirical Bernstein bound)**, Corollary 5 (empirical Bernstein, finite class), Theorem 6 (covering-number version). Confirmed in the rendered PDF text: "Theorem 4 Under the conditions of Theorem 1 we have with probability at least 1−δ ...".

(2) EXACT STATEMENT OF THEOREM 4 (verbatim from the .tex source, p. 2 of the PDF, top of right column area):

"Theorem 4  Under the conditions of Theorem 1 we have with probability at least $1-\delta$ in the i.i.d. vector $\mathbf{Z}=\left( Z_{1},\dots,Z_{n}\right)$ that
    $\mathbb{E}Z-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{i}\leq \sqrt{\frac{2V_{n}\left( \mathbf{Z}\right) \ln 2/\delta }{n}}+\frac{7\ln 2/\delta }{3\left( n-1\right) },$
where $V_{n}\left( \mathbf{Z}\right)$ is the sample variance
    $V_{n}\left( \mathbf{Z}\right) =\frac{1}{n\left( n-1\right) }\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\left( Z_{i}-Z_{j}\right) ^{2}.$"

In plain notation:
    E[Z] − (1/n)·Σ_{i=1}^n Z_i  ≤  sqrt( 2·V_n(Z)·ln(2/δ) / n )  +  7·ln(2/δ) / (3(n−1)).

(3) RANGE ASSUMPTION. "Under the conditions of Theorem 1" = Theorem 1 (Hoeffding's inequality): "Let $Z,Z_{1},\dots,Z_{n}$ be i.i.d. random variables with values in $\left[ 0,1\right]$ and let $\delta >0$." So: i.i.d., values in the UNIT interval [0,1], δ > 0. No explicit n ≥ 2 appears in Theorem 4's own statement, but n ≥ 2 is required for V_n and 1/(n−1) to be defined; the supporting Theorem 10 states "Let $n\geq 2$" explicitly, and Corollary 5 states "For $\delta >0,$ $n\geq 2$".

(4) SAMPLE VARIANCE: UNBIASED, n−1 DENOMINATOR. The pairwise form V_n(Z) = [1/(n(n−1))]·Σ_{i<j}(Z_i−Z_j)^2 is algebraically identical to (1/(n−1))·Σ_i (Z_i − Z̄)^2, i.e. the UNBIASED sample variance (ddof=1). I verified this numerically (n=9 random sample: pairwise form = 0.1062638687471244 = np.var(z, ddof=1); the biased ddof=0 value was 0.09445677). So E[V_n] = V(Z) exactly in the i.i.d. case.

(5) CONFIDENCE TERM: ln(2/δ), NOT ln(1/δ). Both occurrences in Theorem 4 are ln 2/δ (natural log). The factor 2 comes from a union bound in the proof (Bennett applied at level δ/2 combined with the standard-deviation bound (3)/"Stdev upper bound" at level δ/2). Contrast: their Theorem 1 (Hoeffding) and Theorem 3 (Bennett) both use ln 1/δ, since those need no union bound. The finite-class Corollary 5 has ln(2|F|/δ) in both terms.

(6) ONE-SIDED AS STATED. Theorem 4 is written as a one-sided inequality bounding EZ above by the empirical mean plus the deviation term (equivalently, a lower deviation bound for the empirical mean). The paper's explicit symmetry remarks are attached to Theorem 1 ("Replacing $Z$ by $1-Z$ shows that the confidence interval is symmetric about $\mathbb{E}Z$") and Theorem 3 ("The bound is symmetric about $\mathbb{E}Z$") — NO such remark follows Theorem 4. Since V_n(1−Z) = V_n(Z), the mirrored one-sided bound also holds at level δ, but making the interval two-sided costs another union bound: the standard two-sided form uses ln(4/δ). This is exactly how Waudby-Smith & Ramdas restate it (arXiv:2010.09686, Appendix, "EB-CI [MP09]"): "(1/n)Σ X_i ± sqrt(2σ̂²log(4/α)/n) + 7log(4/α)/(3(n−1)), and σ̂² is the sample variance."

(7) CONSTANT 7/(3(n−1)) — CONFIRMED VERBATIM. The LaTeX is literally `\frac{7\ln 2/\delta }{3\left( n-1\right) }`. It is 7/3 divided by (n−1), NOT 7/(3n). Note the asymmetry the paper deliberately uses: the leading (square-root) term has denominator n, while the second-order term has denominator n−1.

(8) GENERAL (NON-IDENTICALLY-DISTRIBUTED) VERSION — Theorem 11, same constants: "Let $\mathbf{X}=(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ be a vector of independent random variables with values in $[0,1]$. Let $\delta >0$. Then with probability at least $1-\delta$ in $\mathbf{X}$ we have $\mathbb{E}[P_n(\mathbf{X})] \leq P_n(\mathbf{X}) + \sqrt{\frac{2V_n(\mathbf{X})\ln 2/\delta}{n}} + \frac{7\ln 2/\delta}{3(n-1)}$." The text says it "reduces to Theorem 4 for identically distributed variables."

(9) SUPPORTING Theorem 10 (standard-deviation bounds, each one-sided at level δ, ln 1/δ): "Let $n\geq 2$ and $\mathbf{X}=(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ be a vector of independent random variables with values in $[0,1]$. Then for $\delta>0$ we have ... $\Pr\{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}V_n} > \sqrt{V_n(\mathbf{X})} + \sqrt{\frac{2\ln 1/\delta}{n-1}}\} \leq \delta$ and $\Pr\{\sqrt{V_n(\mathbf{X})} > \sqrt{\mathbb{E}V_n} + \sqrt{\frac{2\ln 1/\delta}{n-1}}\} \leq \delta$."

(10) Related, for context: Corollary 5 (finite class) = sqrt(2V_n(f,X)ln(2|F|/δ)/n) + 7ln(2|F|/δ)/(3(n−1)) ∀f∈F; Theorem 6 (polynomial growth, requires n ≥ 16, M(n) = 10·N_∞(1/n,F,2n)) = sqrt(18V_n(f,X)ln(M(n)/δ)/n) + 15ln(M(n)/δ)/(n−1).
checks.corrections:
Nothing in the claim is wrong — every element checks out (Theorem 4, ln(2/δ), 7/(3(n−1)), unbiased n−1 sample variance, one-sided). Precision points to get right in the paper:

1. RANGE IS [0,1], NOT GENERAL [a,b]. Theorem 4 assumes values in the unit interval. If your losses live in [0,R] (or an interval of width R), you must rescale: E Z − Z̄ ≤ sqrt(2 V_n(Z) ln(2/δ)/n) + 7R·ln(2/δ)/(3(n−1)), where V_n is in the original (unrescaled) units. Only the second term picks up R; the first term is scale-correct as written because V_n scales as R². Stating the bound for "bounded random variables" without naming the range is the single most common citation error.

2. THE TWO DENOMINATORS DIFFER ON PURPOSE. First term: n. Second term: n−1. Do not "tidy" both to n or both to n−1. Writing 7ln(2/δ)/(3n) is a misquote (and is not implied by the theorem).

3. ONE-SIDED vs TWO-SIDED. As stated it is one-sided. If you present a two-sided confidence interval, the honest statement replaces ln(2/δ) with ln(4/δ) in BOTH terms (union bound over the two directions, applying the theorem to Z and to 1−Z, which leaves V_n unchanged). Do not cite "Maurer & Pontil Theorem 4" for a ± interval with ln(2/δ) — that is a coverage-losing misstatement.

4. "SAMPLE VARIANCE" MUST BE THE UNBIASED ONE. The paper writes it in the U-statistic/pairwise form [1/(n(n−1))]Σ_{i<j}(Z_i−Z_j)², which equals (1/(n−1))Σ(Z_i−Z̄)², i.e. ddof=1 / Bessel-corrected. Plugging in the biased (1/n) estimator makes the stated bound formally invalid (it is anti-conservative by a factor n/(n−1) inside the square root). In code: np.var(x, ddof=1), not np.var(x).

5. n ≥ 2 IS NEEDED (implicitly). Theorem 4 inherits only "i.i.d. in [0,1], δ>0" from Theorem 1, but n ≥ 2 is required for V_n and 1/(n−1); the companion Theorem 10 and Corollary 5 state n ≥ 2 explicitly. State n ≥ 2 when you quote it.

6. logs are NATURAL logs. ln, not log₂ or log₁₀.

7. δ RANGE. Theorem 4 says only "δ > 0" (a vacuous-but-valid convention for δ ≥ 1); Theorem 6 restricts to δ ∈ (0,1). Use δ ∈ (0,1).

8. ATTRIBUTION NUANCE. Their Theorem 3 is labeled "Bennett's inequality" (not Bernstein's) — E Z − Z̄ ≤ sqrt(2 V Z ln(1/δ)/n) + ln(1/δ)/(3n) with the TRUE variance. Also, the paper explicitly credits an "analogous result" to Audibert, Munos & Szepesvári and claims only "a slightly better constant" plus a new proof technique — so do not describe Maurer & Pontil as introducing the empirical Bernstein bound; describe them as giving improved constants (which is exactly how their own abstract puts it: "We give improved constants for data dependent and variance sensitive confidence bounds, called empirical Bernstein bounds").

9. THE COROLLARY CONSTANTS CHANGE. If you need a uniform-over-class version, do not reuse 7/(3(n−1)) with covering numbers: Corollary 5 (finite F) keeps 2 and 7/3 but with ln(2|F|/δ); Theorem 6 (polynomial growth) degrades to 18 inside the root and 15/(n−1) outside, and requires n ≥ 16.

RECOMMENDED PHRASING (one-sided, matches the source exactly):

"We use the empirical Bernstein bound of Maurer and Pontil [2009, Theorem 4]. Let Z_1,…,Z_n be i.i.d. with values in [0,1], n ≥ 2, and δ ∈ (0,1). Then with probability at least 1 − δ,

checks.corrections:
Your claim is close but has four specific inaccuracies. Fix all four before the paper goes out.

1. THE RATE CONDITION IS NOT "(log(pn))^7 / n -> 0". Two errors:
   (a) The envelope B_n is missing. The actual condition in Corollary 2.1, Corollary 3.1, and condition (M) of Theorem 5.1 is B_n^2 (log(pn))^7 / n <= C_2 n^{-c_2} under (E.1)/(E.3), or B_n^4 (log(pn))^7 / n <= C_2 n^{-c_2} under (E.2)/(E.4). B_n is explicitly allowed to diverge, and the paper stresses (Comment 2.5) that "in applications B_n typically grows at a fractional power of n". Dropping B_n silently assumes the sub-exponential-with-fixed-constant case, where you may set B_n = C_1 and the condition does reduce to (log(pn))^7 / n <= C n^{-c}.
   (b) It is not "-> 0"; it is a POLYNOMIAL-rate requirement "<= C_2 n^{-c_2}" for some c_2 > 0. That strengthening is exactly what buys the polynomial error bound C n^{-c}; a bare "-> 0" would only give o(1). The literal "-> 0" form appears once, in Comment 2.5, and it is B_n^6 (log(pn))^7 / n -> 0, attached to the deliberately crude Lemma 2.3, which the authors describe as "only useful in some limited cases". Do not cite that as the paper's condition.
   The nearest thing to your intended phrasing that IS in the paper is Comment 5.1: "(log p)^7 <= C_2 n^{1-c_2} for arbitrarily small c_2", i.e. log p nearly of order n^{1/7}.

2. THE VARIANCE CONDITION IS TWO-SIDED AND IS AN AVERAGE OVER i, NOT "min_j E[x_ij^2] >= c_1". The paper's condition, in (E.1), (E.2), Lemma 2.3, Theorem 3.1, and Theorem 3.2, is: c_1 <= Ebar[x_ij^2] <= C_1 for all 1 <= j <= p, where Ebar[.] := E_n[E[.]] = n^{-1} sum_{i=1}^n E[.]. So (i) there is an upper bound C_1 as well as the lower bound c_1 — your version drops it, and C_1 appears in the constants of every conclusion; (ii) the quantity bounded is the time-average n^{-1} sum_i E[x_ij^2] of the coordinatewise second moments, not each individual E[x_ij^2] (this matters under heteroskedasticity/non-identical distributions, which the paper allows). Only in (E.3)/(E.4) and Comment 2.2 does a one-sided lower bound appear (E[eps_ij^2] >= c_1, Ebar[x_ij^2] >= c_1), and there it is paired with a separate moment bound.

3. COROLLARY 3.1 CARRIES AN EXTRA HYPOTHESIS YOU DID NOT MENTION. It also requires the approximation conditions (14)-(15) to hold with zeta_1 sqrt(log p) + zeta_2 <= C_2 n^{-c_2}. If your statistic is an exact average (T = T_0, W = W_0), this is vacuous — take zeta_1 = zeta_2 = 0 — and you should say so explicitly in your paper, since a reader checking Corollary 3.1 will otherwise think you skipped a condition. If your statistic is only an approximate average (the usual case in post-selection / influence-function settings, e.g. a linearization with remainder), you MUST verify (14)-(15) at that rate; that verification is the substantive work, not a technicality.

4. "STUDENTIZED" IS FLATLY WRONG FOR THIS PAPER. CCK (2013, AoS) never studentizes. The word does not occur in the paper at all. T_0 = max_j n^{-1/2} sum_i x_ij is a raw maximum of sums; the bootstrap statistic W_0 = max_j n^{-1/2} sum_i x_ij e_i is likewise unnormalized; and the multiple-testing application in Section 5 uses t_j := sqrt(n)(betahat_j - beta_{0j}), with no sigmahat_j in the denominator. Do not attribute a studentized-max result to CCK (2013).

ON QUESTION (2) SPECIFICALLY — WHICH NUMBER TO CITE:
- Corollary 3.1 IS the right citation for "the multiplier bootstrap critical value is valid, with error C n^{-c}, under primitive moment conditions". That is its exact role: it is the primitive-condition specialization of Theorems 2.2 and 3.2 to the leading examples (E.1)-(E.4). Its title is literally "Multiplier Bootstrap in Leading Examples". Cite it.
- Corollary 2.1 is WRONG for a bootstrap claim: it is Gaussian approximation only (rho <= C n^{-c}, with rho comparing T_0 to the Gaussian analogue Z_0). No bootstrap appears in it.
- Theorem 3.1 / Theorem 3.2 are the correct citations if you want the NON-ASYMPTOTIC, assumption-light versions: 3.1 for exact means, 3.2 for approximate means. They hold under only c_1 <= Ebar[x_ij^2] <= C_1 (plus (14)-(15) for 3.2), but their bounds are stated in terms of rho, pi(theta), P(Delta > theta), zeta_1, zeta_2 — quantities you then have to bound yourself. Cite 3.1/3.2 when you need the finite-sample bound; cite 3.1+Corollary 3.1 together when you want "valid with polynomial rate under primitive conditions". Standard practice in the literature is Theorem 3.2 + Corollary 3.1 as a pair.
- The word "uniformly" does NOT appear in Corollary 3.1. Uniformity there is implicit and real but should be phrased carefully: the bound is non-asymptotic and its constants c, C "depend only on c_1, C_1, c_2, and C_2", hence it holds uniformly over any class of DGPs satisfying those conditions with COMMON constants. Say it that way. If you want a result the authors themselves state as uniform over a class of data-generating processes, that is Theorem 5.1 (strong FWER control for the Romano-Wolf stepdown with multiplier bootstrap critical values), which says "uniformly over a class of data-generating processes Omega". For a post-selection paper doing simultaneous inference, Theorem 5.1 is very likely the result you actually want to lean on.

ON QUESTION (3): CCK (2013, AoS) covers ONLY the non-studentized statistic. For the studentized max, cite Chernozhukov, Chetverikov & Kato, "Inference on Causal and Structural Parameters using Many Moment Inequalities", Review of Economic Studies 86(5):1867-1900 (2019) — arXiv:1312.7614, originally circulated as "Testing many moment inequalities" — specifically Theorem 4.3 and Comment 4.6. Note the title change: if you cite "Testing many moment inequalities" you must flag it as the earlier working-paper title of the RESTUD article, or a referee will call it a phantom reference. Do NOT substitute CCK (2017, AoP): that paper generalizes the index set to hyperrectangles and sparsely convex sets and improves the rate to n^{-1/6}, but it is also non-studentized (zero occurrences of "studenti" in the full text). CCK's own Comment 4.6 in the RESTUD paper draws exactly this line, describing their studentized result as complementing "a high dimensional bootstrap CLT for non-studentized sample averages derived in Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, and Kato (2013) and Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, and Kato (2017)."

A. NON-STUDENTIZED MAX, primitive conditions (most likely what you want if you never divide by sigmahat_j):
"Validity of the Gaussian multiplier bootstrap critical value for the maximum of a high-dimensional sum follows from Chernozhukov, Chetverikov and Kato (2013, Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.1). B. IF YOUR STATISTIC IS ONLY AN APPROXIMATE AVERAGE (linearization with a remainder — typical for post-selection influence-function arguments):
"...we apply Chernozhukov, Chetverikov and Kato (2013, Theorem 3.2), verifying their approximation conditions (14)-(15) with zeta_1 sqrt(log p) + zeta_2 = O(n^{-c_2}); Corollary 3.1 then yields sup_alpha |P(T <= c_W(alpha)) - alpha| <= C n^{-c}."

SOURCING NOTE: The published REStat PDF (direct.mit.edu), the SSRN PDF, and a third-party mirror are all paywalled/403. I therefore quote the authors' own working-paper version, NBER Technical Working Paper 344 (the CGM 2008 working paper), which I fetched and text-extracted in full, and I cross-checked its content against the same authors' later survey, Cameron & Miller (2015, JHR), which restates the CGM 2008 procedure. Section numbers below are from TWP 344; the published article's corresponding sections are Roman-numbered (III.B, III.C, etc.).

=== (A) CAMERON, GELBACH & MILLER (2008) ===

A1. Wild cluster bootstrap DGP, TWP 344 §3.2 ("Residual and Wild Cluster Bootstrap-t"). The procedure creates pseudo-samples in which the cluster residual vector û_g is kept with probability 0.5 and sign-flipped (−û_g) with probability 0.5, "with this assignment at the cluster level." X is held fixed across resamples.

A2. Multipliers, TWP 344 §3.2, verbatim: "The weights we use (+1 with probability 0.5 and −1 with probability 0.5) are called Rademacher weights." So YES — Rademacher two-point weights are what they use and recommend.

A3. Footnote 8 to that sentence: the weights "lead to asymptotic refinement if β̂ is symmetrically distributed"; if β̂ is asymmetrically distributed "our version is still asymptotically valid, but different weights provide asymptotic refinement," and they note that Davidson and Flachaire (2001) "provide theory and simulation to nonetheless support using Rademacher weights even in the asymmetric case."

A4. The full recommended algorithm is in Appendix A.2, "Wild Cluster bootstrap-t with H0 imposed." It inherits steps 1 and 3 from the cluster residual bootstrap-t with H0 imposed and replaces step 2a. Reconstructed:
  Step 1. On the original sample form w = (β̂₁ − β₁⁰)/s_β̂₁, where s_β̂₁ comes from the cluster-robust variance estimator (their eq. 3) using ũ_g = √(G/(G−1))·û_g. Also obtain the RESTRICTED OLS estimator β̂^R imposing H₀: β₁ = β₁⁰, and its restricted residuals {û₁^R, …, û_G^R}. (Their footnote 13: the restricted estimator is obtained by regressing y_ig − β₁⁰x₁,ig on a constant and all regressors other than x₁,ig.)
  Step 2a (the wild step, verbatim structure). For each cluster g = 1,…,G, form either û_g^R* = û_g^R with probability 0.5 or û_g^R* = −û_g^R with probability 0.5, and then form ŷ_g* = X_g′β̂^R + û_g^R*.
  Step 2b. On each pseudo-sample run UNRESTRICTED OLS and compute w_b* = (β̂*₁,b − β₁⁰)/s_β̂*₁,b, with s computed "using the same method as that in step 1" (i.e., the same CRVE).
  Step 3, verbatim: "Reject H0 at level α if and only if w < w*[α/2] or w > w*[1−α/2]", where w*[q] is the qth quantile of w₁*,…,w_B*. (Note: this is the EQUAL-TAILED rule. The symmetric version — p = fraction of b with |w_b*| > |w| — is what Cameron & Miller (2015, §VI.C.2) present and what most software defaults to.)

A5. Mammen alternative, TWP 344 Appendix A.2: after defining Rademacher weights they state that Mammen (1993) proposed a_g = (1−√5)/2 ≈ −0.6180 with probability (1+√5)/(2√5) ≈ 0.7236, and a_g = 1 − (1−√5)/2 otherwise; these are "the only two-point distribution that satisfy the constraints E[a_g] = 0 and E[a²_g] = 1 and the additional constraint E[a³_g] = 1", the last being needed for refinement when β̂ is asymmetrically distributed. They do NOT adopt Mammen weights.

A6. What they recommend overall, TWP 344 conclusion: the wild cluster bootstrap "does especially well," and "The variation we use is one that uses equal weights and probability, and uses residuals from OLS estimation that imposes the null hypothesis." Also: "provided the same method is used in calculating the Wald statistic in the original sample and in the bootstrap resamples."

A7. Number of replications, TWP 344 §4: "For bootstraps we used B = 399 bootstraps rather than the recommended B = 999 or higher." (399 was a Monte-Carlo-cost concession, not a recommendation.)

A8. ON SMALL G — what they actually say. Published abstract (via NBER/RePEc landing pages): standard asymptotic tests "can over-reject … with few (five to thirty) clusters". TWP 344 §5: the residual and wild cluster bootstrap methods "perform well in cases with as few as 6 clusters." Conclusion: "Using the wild cluster bootstrap-t method our empirical rejection rates are extremely close to the theoretical values, even with as few as six clusters." Abstract also: "we consider examples with as few as five clusters."

A9. ON THE 2^G LIMITATION — the ONLY thing CGM 2008 says. TWP 344 §3.3 ("Bootstraps with Few Clusters"), verbatim: "With few clusters the bootstrap resampling methods produce a distinctly finite number of possible pseudo-samples, so the bootstrap distribution w₁*,…,w_q* will not be smooth even with many bootstrap replications." I grepped the entire extracted text for "2^G", "2G", "distinct", "enumerat", "rule of thumb", "30 or more", "50 or more": there is NO 2^G statement, NO enumeration discussion, and NO G ≥ 30 (or any other) rule of thumb anywhere in the paper.

A10. The 2^G result belongs to Cameron & Miller (2015, JHR 50(2):317–372), §VI.C.2, verbatim: "Because this is done across G clusters, there are at most 2^G possible combinations of the data, so there are at most 2^G unique values of w₁*,…,w_B*. If there are very few clusters then there is no need to actually bootstrap as we can simply enumerate, with separate estimation for each of the 2^G possible datasets." And, crediting Webb: "Webb (2013) expands on these limitations. He shows that there are actually only 2^(G−1) possible t-statistics in absolute value. Thus with G = 5 there are at most 2⁴ = 16 possible values of w₁*,…,w_B*." They add: "As G gets to be as large as 11 this concern is less of an issue since 2^10 = 1024," and that Webb's six-point distribution "is the preferred method to use if G < 10."

A11. Same result in MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb (2023, J. Econometrics 232(2):272–299), §5.3, verbatim: "For the Rademacher distribution, or any other two-point distribution, the number of possible bootstrap samples is just 2^G." And: "Whenever either 2^G (for Rademacher) or 6^G (for six-point) is smaller than the chosen value of B, we can enumerate all possible bootstrap samples instead of drawing them at random. For example, when G = 16, there are just 65,536 Rademacher bootstrap samples to enumerate." They also recommend "at least one variant of the WCR bootstrap (preferably with at least B = 9,999) almost all the time."

A12. The nearest thing to a "G rule of thumb" in this literature — Cameron & Miller (2015), §VI.A, verbatim: "there is no specific point at which we need to worry about few clusters. Instead, 'more is better'. Current consensus appears to be that G = 50 is enough for state-year panel data." And: "there is no clear-cut definition of 'few'. Depending on the situation 'few' may range from less than 20 clusters to less than 50 clusters in the balanced case, and even more clusters in the unbalanced case."

=== (B) DESIGN EFFECT ===

B1. UN Statistics Division, "Household Sample Surveys in Developing and Transition Countries," Chapter VI (Kalton, Brick & Lê), p. 105, eq. (17)–(18), verbatim: V(ȳ_cl) = (S²/n)[1 + (b − 1)ρ], and "The design effect in this simple situation is D²(ȳ_cl) = 1 + (b − 1)ρ". Symbol definition, verbatim: "the design effect from clustering the sample within PSUs depends on two factors: the subsample size within selected PSUs (b) and the intra-class correlation (ρ)." Setup stated just above: A PSUs each containing B households, a SRS of a PSUs, and a SRS of b households within each selected PSU, epsem, first-stage fpc negligible. So b IS the number of sampled observations (elements) per cluster.

B2. Same chapter, p. 119: "Kish (1965) coined the term 'design effect' to denote the ratio of the variance of any statistic under the actual complex sample design to the variance from an SRS or unrestricted sample of the same size."

B3. Unequal cluster sizes, same chapter, eq. (20)–(21): with modest variation use D² = 1 + (b̄ − 1)ρ "with b being replaced by the average subsample size", b̄ = Σb_α/a, "and b_α is the number of elementary units in PSU α". When variation is substantial, Holt (1980) replaces b̄ by b′ = Σb_α² / Σb_α. Their worked example: subsample sizes 10, 10, 20, 20, 40 with ρ = 0.05 give b̄ = 20 and b′ = 26, hence deff = 1.95 by eq. (20) versus 2.25 by eq. (21).

B4. Gabler, Häder & Lahiri (1999), Survey Methodology 25(1), pp. 105–106 (Statistics Canada, cat. 12-001-X), state Kish's combined weighting-plus-clustering formula as deff_Kish = m·(Σw_i²m_i)/(Σw_i m_i)²·[1 + (b̄ − 1)ρ], where "b̄ is the average cluster size and ρ is the intraclass correlation coefficient." Their abstract: "the well-known formula for the design effect intuitively proposed by Kish has a model-based justification. The formula can be interpreted as a conservative value for the actual design effect." Their model-based derivation returns 1 + (b* − 1)ρ with b* = Σ_c(Σ_i w_i m_ic)²/Σ_i w_i²m_i, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives b* ≤ the Kish b̄-form being conservative. With equal weights this collapses to 1 + (b̄ − 1)ρ.

B5. Page citation for Kish. The Wikipedia/Wikiversity "Design effect" article (a heavily sourced tertiary source) attributes the cluster-sampling design effect to Kish 1965, p. 162 — "formulas for the design effect of cluster sampling (with intraclass correlation);[1]:162" — with n* = average cluster size and ρ the ICC, and separately attributes the unequal-weights formula to p. 427 and effective sample size to pp. 162, 259. A ScienceDirect Topics excerpt independently gives "1 + ρ(B−1) … the number of observations within a cluster, B, less one (Kish, 1965, p. 162)." I could not obtain Kish (1965) itself (out-of-print book, not online), so p. 162 rests on concordant secondary/tertiary attribution, not direct inspection.

B6. Independent peer-reviewed restatement: Killip, Mahfoud & Pearce (2004), "What Is an Intracluster Correlation Coefficient?", Annals of Family Medicine 2(3):204–208 (PMC1466680), eq. 2, verbatim: "DE = 1 + ρ(m − 1)", with ρ the intracluster correlation coefficient and m "the number of subjects in a cluster", stated for the special case of equal-sized groups.

B7. The regression analogue (relevant if you apply this to a regression coefficient rather than a mean) — Cameron & Miller (2015), eq. (6), verbatim: "τ_k ≃ 1 + ρ_xk ρ_u (N̄_g − 1)", where ρ_xk is the within-cluster correlation of the regressor, ρ_u the within-cluster error correlation, N̄_g the average cluster size. They add: "The result (6) is exact if clusters are of equal size ('balanced' clusters) and ρ_xk = 1 for all regressors (Kloek, 1981)", and for unequal sizes replace (N̄_g − 1) by (V[N_g]/N̄_g + N̄_g − 1), citing "Moulton (1986, p.387)".
checks.corrections:
(A) THREE THINGS TO FIX.

1. CORRECT as stated: the recommended procedure is the wild CLUSTER bootstrap-t with the null hypothesis IMPOSED (restricted residuals from the null-constrained OLS fit), X held fixed, one multiplier per cluster applied to the whole cluster residual vector, unrestricted OLS on each pseudo-sample, CRVE standard errors computed the SAME way in the original sample and every resample, and the bootstrap distribution of the t/Wald statistic (not of β̂, and not a bootstrap standard error) used for the test. Do not describe it as a "bootstrap standard error" method — CGM are emphatic that bootstrap-se gives no asymptotic refinement.

2. CORRECT as stated: Rademacher two-point weights (+1 / −1 each with probability 0.5). Two refinements worth carrying: (a) CGM note these give asymptotic refinement only when β̂ is symmetrically distributed, and cite Davidson & Flachaire in support of using Rademacher anyway in the asymmetric case; (b) Mammen's (1993) two-point weights are discussed as the alternative that additionally satisfies E[a³]=1, but CGM do not adopt them. Also note CGM's Appendix uses the EQUAL-TAILED rejection rule (w outside the α/2 and 1−α/2 bootstrap quantiles), whereas the symmetric |w| rule is what Cameron & Miller (2015) and most software (boottest, Stata's wildbootstrap) use. If your paper says "we follow CGM (2008)", say which of the two you actually did.

3. WRONG — the two claims about G are both misattributed to CGM (2008):
   (a) There is NO "G ≥ 30" rule of thumb in CGM (2008), and no numeric threshold of any kind. Their "(five to thirty) clusters" phrase in the abstract is the range over which STANDARD ASYMPTOTIC tests over-reject, i.e. the problem region their method is designed to fix — not a minimum G for using the method. Their headline finding is the opposite of a G ≥ 30 requirement: the wild cluster bootstrap-t achieves near-nominal size "even with as few as six clusters." If you want a threshold, the citable statement is Cameron & Miller (2015, JHR, §VI.A): "Current consensus appears to be that G = 50 is enough for state-year panel data," together with their explicit disclaimer that there is no clear-cut definition of "few" (roughly <20 to <50 balanced, more if unbalanced). Attribute that to Cameron & Miller (2015), not CGM (2008).
   (b) There is NO 2^G statement in CGM (2008). The paper only says, in §3.3, that with few clusters there is "a distinctly finite number of possible pseudo-samples" so the bootstrap distribution "will not be smooth" — it never writes 2^G, never discusses enumeration, and never notes the induced p-value granularity. The 2^G result and its consequences are due to Webb (QED Working Paper 1315, 2013; published as Webb, "Reworking wild bootstrap-based inference for clustered errors," Canadian Journal of Economics 56(3):839–858, 2023), and are stated as 2^G in Cameron & Miller (2015, §VI.C.2) and MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb (2023, J. Econometrics 232(2):272–299, §5.3). Also get the exponent right: there are 2^G distinct bootstrap SAMPLES, but only 2^(G−1) distinct |t|-statistics, because flipping every sign simultaneously leaves |t| unchanged — so the finest attainable two-sided p-value is 1/2^(G−1), i.e. 0.0625 at G = 5, not 1/2^G. Practical corollaries you can cite: enumerate rather than sample whenever 2^G < B (boottest does this by default); use Webb's six-point distribution when G < 10; and MNW recommend B ≥ 9,999 when you do sample.

(B) FORMULA CORRECT; FOUR CAVEATS.

1. DEFF = 1 + (m − 1)ρ is correct and standard, and m IS the number of observations (elements) sampled per cluster — confirmed independently in the UN handbook chapter (b = "subsample size within selected PSUs"), in Killip et al. (m = "the number of subjects in a cluster"), and in Gabler et al. (b̄ = "the average cluster size"). It is not the number of clusters.

2. Conditions. The formula is exact only for: a common cluster size m, an epsem (self-weighting) design, a common ρ across clusters, negligible fpc, and the estimator being a MEAN (or proportion/total under the same conditions). Say "cluster sample mean," not "estimator" generically.

3. Unequal cluster sizes. Substituting the mean size m̄ is an approximation and is anti-conservative. The sharper approximation (Holt 1980) replaces m̄ with m′ = Σ_g m_g² / Σ_g m_g, which is ≥ m̄ and equals m̄ only when sizes are equal. The UN chapter's example makes the gap concrete: sizes {10,10,20,20,40} with ρ = 0.05 give deff = 1.95 using m̄ = 20 versus 2.25 using m′ = 26. If your clusters are unbalanced (they usually are in ML eval data), cite the m′ form or state explicitly that you are using the equal-size idealization.

4. Do not apply it to a regression coefficient. DEFF = 1 + (m−1)ρ is the mean case. For a regression slope the correct inflation is the Moulton factor τ_k ≈ 1 + ρ_x ρ_u (m̄ − 1), where ρ_x is the within-cluster correlation of the REGRESSOR and ρ_u that of the ERROR. The Kish form is the special case ρ_x = 1 (a cluster-invariant regressor, e.g. the constant, i.e. the mean). Using 1 + (m−1)ρ for a coefficient on an individual-level regressor with low within-cluster correlation will badly overstate the variance inflation. Sign note: ρ can in principle be negative (bounded below near −1/(m−1)), giving DEFF < 1; the sources note this is rare in practice for real survey variables.

5. Attribution wording. Kish (1965) coined "design effect" and gave the cluster-sampling formula; the page most commonly cited for it is p. 162. I could not inspect the book directly (not available online), so if you want the page number in your paper, either cite it as "Kish (1965, p. 162)" following the standard secondary attribution or drop the page and cite the book. Kish's own notation writes it as deff = 1 + roh(b̄ − 1), where "roh" is his mnemonic for the rate of homogeneity (= ρ). Also note Kish (1987/1995) is the correct cite for the COMBINED weighting-and-clustering formula (the Σw²m / (Σwm)² prefactor), not Kish (1965).

(A) WILD CLUSTER BOOTSTRAP

Cite:
Cameron, A. C., J. B. Gelbach, and D. L. Miller (2008). "Bootstrap-Based Improvements for Inference with Clustered Errors." Review of Economics and Statistics 90(3): 414–427. doi:10.1162/rest.90.3.414.
Webb, M. D. (2023). "Reworking wild bootstrap-based inference for clustered errors." Canadian Journal of Economics 56(3): 839–858. doi:10.1111/caje.12661. [Working paper: Queen's Economics Dept. WP 1315, 2013.]
Cameron, A. C., and D. L. Miller (2015). "A Practitioner's Guide to Cluster-Robust Inference." Journal of Human Resources 50(2): 317–372.
MacKinnon, J. G., M. Ø. Nielsen, and M. D. Webb (2023). "Cluster-robust inference: A guide to empirical practice." Journal of Econometrics 232(2): 272–299.

Suggested paper sentences (drop-in):

"We compute p-values by the wild cluster bootstrap-t of Cameron, Gelbach, and Miller (2008). Residuals are taken from the OLS fit that imposes the null; each cluster's residual vector is multiplied by an independent Rademacher draw (+1 or −1 with probability 1/2), the regressors are held fixed across resamples, and the same cluster-robust variance estimator is used for the original and bootstrap test statistics."

"Because the Rademacher weights admit only 2^G distinct sign assignments — and only 2^(G−1) distinct absolute t-statistics (Webb 2023) — the attainable p-values are discrete at small G; we [enumerate all 2^G assignments / use B = 9,999 draws] as recommended by MacKinnon, Nielsen, and Webb (2023)."

If you need a statement about how many clusters suffice:
"There is no sharp threshold for the number of clusters; Cameron and Miller (2015) report that the current consensus is that G = 50 suffices for state-year panel data, while noting that 'few' may mean anywhere from fewer than 20 to fewer than 50 clusters in the balanced case and more when clusters are unbalanced."

DO NOT write: "Cameron, Gelbach, and Miller (2008) recommend G ≥ 30" (no such statement), or "Cameron, Gelbach, and Miller (2008) note that Rademacher weights permit only 2^G distinct draws" (that result is Webb's; CGM only remark that the number of pseudo-samples is finite and the bootstrap distribution not smooth).

(B) DESIGN EFFECT

Cite:
Kish, L. (1965). Survey Sampling. New York: Wiley. (p. 162 for the cluster-sampling design effect.)
Optionally add, for the unbalanced case: Kalton, G., J. M. Brick, and T. Lê (2005). "Estimating components of design effects for use in sample design," Ch. VI in Household Sample Surveys in Developing and Transition Countries, United Nations, pp. 95–121; and Gabler, S., S. Häder, and P. Lahiri (1999). "A model based justification of Kish's formula for design effects for weighting and clustering." Survey Methodology 25(1): 105–106.
If you are inflating a REGRESSION standard error rather than a mean: Moulton, B. R. (1990). "An Illustration of a Pitfall in Estimating the Effects of Aggregate Variables on Micro Units." Review of Economics and Statistics 72(2): 334–338.

Suggested paper sentence (balanced case):
"For a cluster sample with m observations per cluster and intraclass correlation ρ, the variance of the sample mean is inflated relative to simple random sampling by the design effect DEFF = 1 + (m − 1)ρ (Kish 1965, p. 162)."

Suggested paper sentence (unbalanced case — recommended if your cluster sizes vary):
"With unequal cluster sizes we use DEFF = 1 + (m′ − 1)ρ, where m′ = Σ_g m_g² / Σ_g m_g is the size-weighted mean cluster size (Kish 1965; Kalton, Brick, and Lê 2005, eq. 21); substituting the unweighted mean m̄ understates the inflation."

"For a regression coefficient the corresponding inflation is the Moulton factor 1 + ρ_x ρ_u (m̄ − 1), where ρ_x and ρ_u are the within-cluster correlations of the regressor and the error (Moulton 1990); Kish's DEFF = 1 + (m − 1)ρ is the special case ρ_x = 1."
